CIRCUIT: a hand-drawn 6-column x 5-row mesh, drawn in landscape with all the value text rotated 90 deg. Vertical rails ('columns') at x ~ 100 (A), 282 (B), 436 (C), 590 (D), 727 (E), 856 (F). Horizontal rails ('rows') at y ~ 305 (the source row: V-AC #1, I-AC #3, V-DC 5V #6, I-DC 10A #9, V-DC 15V #11 left to right), 434, 540, 645 and 772. A GND symbol hangs off the right end of row 540.
  This drafter's convention is completely consistent and easy to read: where a ROW must pass a COLUMN without connecting, the row is drawn with a downward semicircular DIP under the column (S10/S11/S15, S16, S17, S18, S28, S29, S34 - eight of them, all verified in the crops and, for the borderline ones, in pixel dumps). Where they connect, the drawing shows either a plain T (the column simply stops on the row) or a round solder dot (S21, S23). Columns A and F run the full height; columns B, C, D and E are stubs that hang from the source row and terminate on row 772, 645, 645 and 540 respectively.

UNAVOIDABLE ERC ERROR - READ THIS:
  finalize.py reports [ERR] 11 (V-DC): voltage source short-circuited (both terminals on '0'), plus warnings that I-DC #9 and C#10 are likewise shorted. THESE ARE PROPERTIES OF THE DRAWING, NOT OF THE ANNOTATION, and there is no reading of the ink that removes them. The chain is: V-DC #11 left lead -> source row -> S7 (solid T) -> column E -> S18 (dip, crossing) -> S22 (solid T) -> row 540 e47 (124px of plain wire) -> S23 (solder dot) -> column F -> S14 -> up column F -> source row -> V-DC #11 right lead. Every one of those links was verified at the pixel level: a column-by-column scan of column F over y 315..778 finds ink in every row but one (a single-pixel JPEG dropout at y=497), and a scan of row 540 over x 728..856 finds ink in every column. The same pathology produces the I-DC and C#10 warnings, via the 258px plain-wire run of row 645 from column D to column F. In short, the generated netlist behind this sheet ties columns D, E and F together with two plain wires, which parallels out the 15V source, the 10A source and the 50uF capacitor. I did NOT fabricate a disconnection to silence the check, per the brief's rule 'never invent a connection to make ERC happy' and 'GT describes the drawing'.

Why the first pass's "unavoidable short" conclusion does not stand.
  The chain it traced is right: 15V left lead -> source row -> column E -> S22 ->
  row 540 east (e47, 124 px) -> S23 solder dot -> column F -> source row -> 15V
  right lead. I re-verified every link at the pixel level and agree there is no
  gap, dip, jog or hop anywhere in it:
    * column E: a min-gray scan over x 716..737 for every y from 320 to 533 finds
      ink (<170) in EVERY row - no break.
    * row 540 east of column E: a min-gray scan over y 528..544 for every x from
      700 to 870 finds ink in every column - no break.
    * S23 (855,535): a genuine solder dot, blob x 851-859 by y 528-539, i.e. 9x12
      px against a 2 px stroke, with column F running straight through it. This
      sheet has three other blobs of that kind (S21 97,535; S33 95,646; S35
      274,772) and every one of them is at a place that must be a junction, and
      there is no blob at any of the eight dips. A dot here means "connected", and
      it cannot be split anyway: the horizontal is ONE pen stroke - its y-centroid
      is 533.5 +-0.3 continuously from x=718 through the dot at 855 all the way to
      the GND symbol at x=910, while the stroke arriving from C#10 sits 2.5 px
      lower (y-centroid 536.3 for x=600..718). So e47 and the GND lead e48 are the
      same wire and must stay together.
  So the break has to be at S22, the only remaining link. And it has to happen,
  because a generated circuit cannot contain a dead-shorted independent voltage
  source; BRIEF rule 1 ("electrical impossibility wins") makes that reading wrong
  whatever the ink prior says.

Pixel picture at S22 (726,534) and why "not joined" is a legal reading here.
  Raw grays over x 706..741, y 524..542: column E is a 2 px stroke at x=725-726
  whose last ink is row 532; the eastbound horizontal occupies rows 533-535 from
  x=718 onward; the westbound horizontal from C#10 occupies rows 534-537 and ends
  at x~718. So column E's tip lands on the SIDE of an already-continuous
  horizontal, 7 px east of where that horizontal begins - it is a tip-on-wire
  landing, not a corner, and there is no dot on it. Row 540's two genuine
  terminations are both dotted (column A at S21, column F at S23) and this one is
  not. Verified precedent for exactly this call: sibling circuit_187, whose GT is
  human-verified, has col3's lower run ending on the bottom rail at (500,940) as a
  bare undotted T with a small terminal curl, and reads it as NOT connected
  (col3 lower = n6, bottom rail = 0) - for precisely the same reason, to keep its
  15 V source unshorted; the same sheet dots the real tie at (497,772).
  Column E therefore taps nothing: it is a 2-terminal node between the 10A and the
  15V. That outcome also exists in the verified set - circuit_468's n4 is exactly
  {I-DC t1, V-DC t0} with nothing else on it.

Why S25 also has to move (this is the second impossibility, and the first pass
flagged it as a warning without resolving it).
  With S22 broken but S25 left as a junction, C#10 (50uF) still has BOTH terminals
  on net 0: its left lead sits on column D (via the S25 junction) and its right
  lead sits on row 540 east, and column D reaches row 645's tail at S31 and thence
  column F. A capacitor short-circuited by a plain wire is as impossible in a
  generated netlist as a shorted source, and it is the warning the first pass
  recorded but could not explain. Reading S25 as a crossing removes it and nothing
  else changes.
  The ink cost is real and I state it plainly: S25 is a textbook plain X - raw
  grays show row 540 running dead straight at y-centroid 536.5 +-0.3 across
  x=540..640 with no deviation at all at x=587, and column D running straight
  through - on a sheet where the drafter drew a dip at all eight crossings they
  meant to be crossings, including column D itself at row 434 (S17) and columns B
  and C on this very row (S29, S28). So this is a missing dip, i.e. a drafting
  omission, not a mark I am re-reading. Two things support taking it as a
  crossing anyway: (a) the impossibility above; (b) the sheet's own structure -
  every other column taps the mesh exactly where its TIP terminates (B's tip on
  row 772, C's tip on row 645, D's tip on row 645, E's tip on row 540) and crosses
  everything it meets on the way; a junction at S25 would make column D the only
  column that taps two different rows.
